desc:
perm is a permutation of the integers 1..n. An inversion is a pair i < j with perm[i] > perm[j]. Return 0 if the number of inversions is even and 1 if it is odd.

You do not need the inversion count itself, only its parity, and this can be found without any sorting.

perm = [2, 1, 3]  -> 1   one inversion (2,1)
perm = [3, 1, 2]  -> 0   two inversions (3,1) (3,2)
perm = [1, 2, 3]  -> 0
hints: You can count all inversions with merge sort in O(n log n), then take the answer modulo 2. Is there something even simpler that only tracks parity?
Swapping any two elements of a permutation changes the parity of its inversion count (the count goes up or down by an odd number). The sorted array has 0 inversions, which is even.
So parity equals the parity of the minimum number of swaps needed to sort the permutation. That number is n - (number of cycles), where cycles are the cycles of the mapping i -> perm[i].
editorial: Exchanging two elements always flips the parity of the inversion count. A permutation that needs s swaps to become sorted can be built from the sorted one by s swaps, so its inversion parity is the parity of s (every way of sorting with swaps uses a number of swaps of the same parity).

The fewest swaps needed to sort a permutation is n - c where c is the number of cycles of the permutation seen as a function i -> perm[i]: a cycle of length L is repaired with L - 1 swaps. Count the cycles with a visited array in O(n) time and take (n - c) % 2.
This is the classic 'sign of a permutation' fact. A merge-sort or Fenwick-tree count followed by % 2 is also correct, but runs in O(n log n).
